cim: Nonprofit advocacy groups cite dangers, sue to stop development of artificial intelligence
cim_eredeti: Nonprofit advocacy groups cite dangers, sue to stop development of artificial intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
A coalition of five nonprofit online safety and advocacy groups filed suit in the San Francisco Superior Court on Thursday, alleging that artificial intelligence (AI) systems are “already autonomously breaking the law and causing harm.” The suit demands an immediate injunction to halt all further development of AI, particularly ChatGPT, Grok, Muse, Gemini, and Claude.

The suit alleges that several Big Tech companies have violated the Business and Professions Code of California’s Unfair Competition Law, specifically the section which prohibits unlawful business practices. Plaintiffs allege that, under the code, AI is a “public nuisance” which the law defines as “[a]nything which is injurious to health . . . or an obstruction to the free use of property, so as to interfere with the comfortable enjoyment of life or property by an entire community or neighborhood.”

Filed by Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative, and Future Tech Insights, doing business as The Alliance For Secure AI, the suit names Big Tech companies Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and SpaceX. “No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products — much less ones that could kill us all — as inevitable,” the plaintiffs wrote.

The complaint quotes Elon Musk, who controls SpaceX and who has invested heavily in AI, as saying that AI “has the potential of civilization destruction.” The complaint also quotes Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, as saying that AI developers “do not understand how our own AI creations work.” Amodei also said that AI could enable a group to carry out a “large-scale biological attack,” which, in a hearing before a subcommittee of the Senate Judiciary Committee, he called “a grave threat to U.S. national security.”

In a press release from Public Citizen, attorney Matthew Platkin who filed the complaint on behalf of the plaintiffs said “It is patently illegal for companies to develop and release products they know are unsafe in any respect, let alone have the potential to exterminate the human race. We are asking the court to intervene before the risks AI executives have warned us about cause devastating and irreversible harm.”

In June, the mother of a Canadian child who died by suicide filed a suit against OpenAI, alleging that its product, ChatGPT, encouraged the girl’s suicide. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI in the same month, alleging that ChatGPT has harmed children by providing information to school shooters, advising children on self-harm, and intentionally addicting children. A group of state attorneys general filed a similar suit in October. In July, Illinois passed legislation that holds AI developers responsible for safety risks, including a requirement for audits of safety issues by independent third parties, with publication of the results.

Guiteau tried for assassinating US President Garfield

On November 14, 1881, Charles Guiteau went on trial for the assassination of US President James A. Garfield. The trial of Guiteau pointed to problems with nineteenth-century law's treatment of insanity; Guiteau's trial is also problematic in retrospect as Garfield's death was immediately attributable not to Guiteau, but to Garfield's doctors who—before sterilization was well understood—repeated probed his wound with unwashed hands while searching for an embedded bullet.
